content:
Hi all,

I’ve just released Econlib, a Lean 4 library for economic and political theory built on mathlib:
https://github.com/danlyng/Econlib. I built this library as foundational infrastructure for formalizing my own research in political economy, so I hope it might be useful to others.

It covers preferences, probability, optimization, game theory, mechanism design, social choice, and
general equilibrium, with worked examples and tests. There is a paper at https://lean4.party/econlib.pdf, though it is written mainly for social scientists rather than for the mathlib audience (I am a PhD candidate in Politics at Princeton so the paper is positioned with that in mind).

Some parts that may be of interest here include supporting formalizations around fixed point
theorems, measurable selection, stochastic orders, Strassen/martingale couplings, optimal transport
and Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality, convex analysis and concavification, KKT/Slater/duality, Berge/
Topkis/Danskin-style results, dynamic programming, Nash existence, Kuhn’s theorem, Arrow-Debreu
equilibrium, Arrow’s theorem, and Gibbard-Satterthwaite.

I also set up Econlib-enabled search tools:

  • Loogle: https://lean4.party/loogle
  • Semantic search: https://lean4.party/search
  • Docs: https://lean4.party/docs

I realize that dropping a large library all at once is not the ideal way to approach potential
mathlib upstreaming, and I don’t expect anyone to review it wholesale. But if there are pieces that
people think would be useful in mathlib, I’d be very happy to split them out, make whatever adjustments are requested, and upstream them through the usual smaller discussion-driven PRs. Feedback on which parts
look most promising, or which design choices would need reworking, would be very welcome.

Note that this is a separate development from the two recently announced EconCSLib projects:
https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16144 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13306. These are focused on economics-and-computation and AI-assisted formalization, respectively--the Econlib project was developed independently and is positioned as a more general formalization-for-theorists library.

I'd be very grateful for your feedback and reactions!

Dan

Is this EconLib project additionally distinct from efforts by AxiomMath in this space? https://www.linkedin.com/posts/axiommath_50-yrs-ago-nobel-prize-winning-economist-activity-7468019861307224066-IXaR/
If the date of the linked post is anything to go by, there are at least two different EconCSLibs which were presented at workshops of the conference EC which are bound to overlap with an EconLib.

There are two projects named EconCSLib; the second of them (at least) discusses their differences: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.16144

On the other hand, there is the confusingly similarly named "EconLib", and there are maybe two of these. There is Dan's EconLib here. There is also AxiomMath's work, e.g. in this paper https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6837298 ; but I am not sure if AxiomMath is actually making a broader "EconLib" (as they hint in that linkedin post).

This is indeed separate from the AxiomMath project. They've since reached out and I'm working with them on their effort.

This is also separate from the two EconCSLib projects. I discuss this a little in the posted paper and have since been in touch with Nikhil, but the intended scope of the EconCSLib projects and my Econlib project are quite different in terms of what they're trying to achieve and what they emphasize.

At any rate this is an exciting time to be interested in formal economic and political theory!

I was thinking about this as worthy project, I didn't realize it already existed. That is good to see, this seems really worth contributing too! Are you planning to maintain it or take more contributions?
I would be interested in substantially contributing to Economics formalization at some point if my schedule permits, so feel free to let me know where this effort goes.
